headline: Showers ease today, then wet, windy systems arrive Monday through Wednesday, with more rain late week.
summary:
Today brings a brief break between systems. Scattered showers over the northern interior and Cascades should fade this evening, with a slight chance (10 to 20 percent) of thunderstorms north of Everett. A ridge of high pressure moves through overnight and dries things out. Highs are expected in the mid to upper 50s.

A new front arrives Monday. Rain reaches the coast by the afternoon and spreads slowly inland into the late afternoon and evening. Southerly winds pick up again, with widespread gusts of 20 to 30 mph possible, though less strong than the recent windy days. Coastal areas and Whidbey Island could see gusts up to 35 mph. Tuesday looks wetter and windier. A long plume of moisture aimed at Vancouver Island moves down through western Washington, with most of the rain aimed at the coast and Olympic Peninsula. Gusts of 35 to 45 mph are possible along the coast and from Whidbey Island northward. Rain and wind continue into Wednesday morning. Forecasters also expect high-elevation mountain snow during this stretch.

The pattern stays unsettled through the end of the week. Scattered showers continue Wednesday and Thursday, with highs warming slightly to the low 60s on Wednesday. Minor coastal flooding may be possible Wednesday morning in the San Juans and Whatcom County because of high tides. Later, an upper-level low near British Columbia is expected to pull moisture toward the region Friday into Saturday, bringing widespread rain and breezy winds into the weekend. Forecasters say they will keep watching this system as it gets closer. River flooding is not expected in the next seven days, though repeated rain will soak the soils. If an atmospheric river stalls over the area late next week into next weekend, the Skokomish River could need watching.

timeline.what: Scattered showers in the northern interior and Cascades taper off, with a slight chance of thunderstorms north of Everett. It dries out overnight under a ridge of high pressure.
A front brings rain to the coast by afternoon, spreading inland later. Southerly winds gust 20 to 30 mph widely, with up to 35 mph on the coast and Whidbey Island.

Another round of widespread rain, mostly aimed at the coast and Olympic Peninsula. Winds strengthen in the afternoon, with gusts of 35 to 45 mph along the coast and from Whidbey Island northward. Rain and wind continue into Wednesday morning.
Unsettled weather with scattered showers. Highs in the low 60s Wednesday. Minor coastal flooding is possible Wednesday morning in the San Juans and Whatcom County due to high tides.
Moisture is funneled toward western Washington from a low near British Columbia, bringing widespread rain and breezy winds into the weekend. Forecasters are still monitoring this system.

timeline.when: Late next week into next weekend
timeline.what: If an atmospheric river stalls over the area, the Skokomish River may need watching. No river flooding is expected in the next seven days.

confidence: Forecasters are fairly confident about the Monday and Tuesday systems, since those are already well defined. They say the Friday-into-Saturday system is still uncertain and will be refined as it approaches. The Skokomish concern depends on whether the atmospheric river stalls, which forecasters describe as a possibility rather than an expectation. For the waves, the chance of seas exceeding 20 feet next weekend is only 30 to 40 percent.
hazards: High Surf Warning until 10 PM tonight for the Grays Harbor County coast and the northern Washington coast.
Gale warnings for Monday on the coastal waters and the east entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, with gusts near 34 knots likely.

Small craft advisories for many marine areas Monday and Tuesday, including Puget Sound, Hood Canal, Admiralty Inlet, the San Juan Islands, and the outer coast. These are warnings for boaters, not for people on land.

glossary.definition: An elongated area of higher air pressure high in the atmosphere. It usually brings drier, calmer weather as it passes.
An elongated area of lower air pressure high in the atmosphere. It tends to bring clouds, showers, and unsettled weather.
A narrow band of concentrated moisture in the atmosphere that can deliver heavy, prolonged rain when it reaches land.
The distance over which wind blows across open water. A long fetch of moisture means a long stretch of ocean feeding moist air toward land.
A forecast of how much precipitation will fall over a given area and time. The discussion uses it to show where the heaviest rain is expected.
A set of computer forecast runs with slightly different starting conditions. When the runs agree, confidence is higher. When they spread apart, the outcome is less certain.
The steady flow of water in a river that comes from groundwater and soil drainage, not from rain runoff. Higher base flow means rivers are more full between storms.
